messages:
Alex: quick heads-up — ran a full-host perf heatmap across the ingest -> parse -> kernel-selector path this morning. results look noisy but one clear hotspot: grpc framing + request parse for streaming chunks is ~45% CPU at p95 for 512-token workloads. plot: https://internal.ci/heatmaps/3187654321.png

Jordan: ugh. do you mean the grpc readv loop or our higher-level proto unmarshal?

Alex: it's the readv+frame-assemble loop (host side) + our parse shims. flame shows big spend in http2/hpack decode and then in Tokenizer::normalize. attached pprof snippet below.

Alex: ```
pprof -nodefraction 0.01 -http=:6060 /tmp/host.prof
# top 20
  45.1%  host-side grpc readv
  21.3%  http2::hpack::decode
  15.8%  tokenizer::normalize_tokens
   8.2%  parser::assemble_stream_chunks
```

Maya: thanks. did you correlate with kvcache hits? sometimes heavy parse + long tail causes extra kvcache lookups because we reify partial prefixes.

Alex: good call — KV cache hit rate for these traces is fine (93%) but we see a spike in kvcache lookup latency when the host CPU is saturated (queueing inside parse path). so it's self-amplifying.

Sam: i'm curious about kernel selection pressure too — are we forcing a bigger kernel for long seqs earlier? that can change decode patterns and backpressure.

Alex: kernel selector logs show a bias: for these request shapes we pick the generic fused-attn kernel because sequence distribution hits a 256+ threshold. suspect our heuristic threshold is too low given host parsing overhead.

Jordan: actionable ideas: 1) raise kernel switch threshold to 384 for the host tier 2) enable an emergency fast-path token-bypass for simple ascii-only inputs 3) reduce grpc chunk assembly copies (use single-buffer writev). which should we try first?

Maya: try 3 then 2. copying is expensive and will reduce the host-side pressure immediately. i can prototype a writev splice in the framer today.

Sam: i'll run a quick canary with kernel threshold bumped to 384 on a subset of hosts (canary id: canary-parse-03). expecting better tail if parse CPU drops below the kernel-switch delta.

ci-bot: triggered benchmark: host-parse-canary/3187654321 started (3 nodes). results ETA ~45m.

Alex: also adding a small batching heuristic tweak — if host_latency > 50ms for parse, shrink batch target by 20% to avoid queuing that amplifies kvcache latency. will open PR.

Jordan: please include a microbenchmark (single-host synthetic) that shows kvcache lookup latency vs parser queue depth. that's the convincing graph for eng-sre.

Maya: putting a draft PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/4827 — implements zero-copy framer + single-writev path for grpc streaming. small benchmark attached in PR notes.

Sam: canary results: 3187654321-canary-03 finished — p95 parse CPU down 18%, end-to-end p99 latency down 12%, kernel-selection flip reduced by ~30% (fewer forced generic kernels).

Alex: nice. Maya's writev change alone accounts for ~10% CPU. i'll merge my batch-shrink heuristic PR after CI.

Jordan: long-term: we should add a parse heatmap to the runtime console so we can correlate kernel choice vs host parse pressure automatically. filing an issue to track. @Maya can you add CI perf check for the framer?

Maya: yup, adding a lightweight p95 check that runs on merge.

Sam: leaving a note — if we bump kernel threshold too high we might regress some GPU-side efficiency for very long contexts. we should gate the change behind a rollout that watches token throughput per-second.

Alex: agreed. rollout plan: (1) merge zero-copy framer (fast rollback) (2) canary kernel threshold increase on 10% fleet (watch token p99 throughput + decode GPU util) (3) batch-shrink heuristic enabled if host parse p95 > 60ms.

Jordan: awesome. ephemeral items: open follow-ups — issue #5942 (console heatmaps), #5943 (canary rollout dashboard) and #5944 (kvcache latency probe).

Alex: thanks team, leaving the thread for updates from the canary and CI benchmarks. :thumbsup:
